questions_and_answers.question: This week's discussion is structured as a debate in which you are assigned to argue against the Debate Proposition - as follows: Debate Proposition: Resolved: The Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment does not justify business decisions, grounded in the personal religious beliefs of owners, that restrict employee rights and access to legally mandated benefits. The focus of this debate is exploring the tension between constitutional rights, business practices, and employee protections as illustrated in U.S. Supreme Court case Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc. Initial Main Post (due Wed. 11:59 pm ET) In your initial main post, present your assigned position against the Debate Proposition. (See background & instructions below.) Background: In Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc., the owners of Hobby Lobby, a closely held corporation, challenged a federal mandate requiring employer-provided health care plans to include coverage for certain types of contraception. The owners objected to this mandate on the grounds of their religious beliefs, arguing that compliance would violate their First Amendment rights under the Free Exercise Clause. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Hobby Lobby, recognizing that closely held corporations could claim protection under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA) to exempt themselves from federal mandates that burden their religious exercise. Debate Instructions: Position Selection: You have been assigned to advocate either the PRO or ADVERSE position on this proposition. You must research and apply critical thinking in advocating for the assigned position. This is not about your personal beliefs but advocating the assigned position in the debate. Argument Development: Each participant must construct a clear and persuasive argument based on the case law, assigned readings, and additional research. Consider the implications of the Hobby Lobby ruling and other relevant cases, such as Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission. Key Issues Relevant to the Debate: Constitutional rights Corporate personhood - businesses as separate entities Corporate social responsibility & stakeholder theory Business ethics Structure Your Debate Contribution - Your Main Post Be succinct. This is not a "paper". Begin with a clear thesis statement that outlines your position. Use evidence from Hobby Lobby, the Horwitz article, and additional scholarly research to support your argument. Briefly address counterarguments to strengthen your case. Summarize your key points and their broader implications. Engage Respectfully: Debate participants are encouraged to challenge opposing views rigorously but respectfully. Focus on the merits of the arguments rather than personal comments. Evaluation Criteria: Logical coherence and persuasiveness of arguments. Depth of analysis and use of supporting evidence. Respectful and constructive engagement with opposing viewpoints. Recommended References: U.S. Supreme Court's majority and dissenting opinions in Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc. (eReserve reading) Horwitz, Paul. "The Hobby Lobby Moment." Harvard Law Review (eReserve reading) Other relevant sections from this week's eReserve readings. Additional research on the interplay between corporate rights, religious freedom, and employee protections. Let the debate begin! Enjoy! The Discussion rubric will be applied according to the (1) following the debate instructions and (2) quality, completeness, and appropriate analysis and relevance of support for your argument.
questions_and_answers.answer: According to Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc., the First Amendment's Free Exercise Clause supports business decisions based on owners' religious convictions, even if those decisions deny employees access to benefits that are required by law, so long as those decisions are safeguarded by the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA). The Supreme Court acknowledged in Hobby Lobby that closely owned companies could exercise their right to practice their religion, protecting their owners from laws that significantly violate their convictions unless the government can demonstrate a compelling interest that is being pursued in the least restrictive way. This ruling highlights the RFRA's goal of protecting religious freedom from needless government interference and making sure that entrepreneurs are not compelled to compromise their beliefs in order to run their companies.The RFRA offers a crucial balance, enabling businesses to preserve their religious identity while meeting the demands of…
